AGENDA
  PLANNING COMMISSION
  NOVEMBER 25, 2024

  SPECIAL MEETING
  NORWALK CITY HALL/COUNCIL CHAMBERS
  6:00 PM

  Linda Lopez, Chair
  Kim Apodaca, Vice Chair
  Rosa Barragan, Planning Commissioner
  Evelyn Nuno, Planning Commissioner
  Lisa Vernola-Salas, Planning Commissioner

Public Comment: The public is encouraged to address the Planning Commission on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other matter
within its jurisdiction subject to the rules and proceedings described in Section 2.16.060 of the Norwalk Municipal Code. If you wish to
address the Planning Commission, please complete the card that is provided at the rear entrance to Council Chambers and hand the card to
the Secretary. The Planning Commission will hear public comment on items listed on the agenda during discussion of the matter and prior to
a vote. The Planning Commission will hear public comment on matters not listed on the agenda during the Oral Communications period.

Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or unless certain emergency or
special circumstances exist. The Planning Commission may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a
future Planning Commission meeting.

Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the Planning Commission:
   Comments should be limited to 3 minutes or less.
   Comments should be directed to the Planning Commission as a whole and not directed to individual Planning Commission members.

Americans with Disabilities Act: In compliance with the ADA, if you need special assistance to participate in a City meeting or other services
offered by this City, please contact the Community Development Department, (562) 929-5744. Assisted listening devices are available at this
meeting. Ask the Secretary if you desire to use this device. Upon request, the agenda and documents in the agenda packet can be made
available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability. Notification of at least 48 hours prior to the meeting or time when
services are needed will assist the City staff in assuring that reasonable arrangements can be made to provide accessibility to the meeting or
service.

Note: Any writings and/or documents provided to a majority of the Planning Commission regarding any item on this agenda after it has been
posted will also be made available for public inspection.
 CALL TO ORDER

FLAG SALUTE

Commissioner Barragan

ROLL CALL OF MEMBERS

MINUTES

REPORTS

  008-902), TO BE IN CONFORMITY WITH THE GENERAL PLAN

  (APN No. 8045-008-902) in the City of Norwalk to be in conformance with the General Plan; and
  2. Consider and find that the project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act pursuant to
  AB 518.

ORAL COMMUNICATIONS

ADJOURNMENT

I, Alexander Hamilton, Interim Director of Community Development/Secretary, hereby certify that the foregoing
agenda was posted at City Hall not less than 72-hours prior to the meeting and forwarded to each member of
the Norwalk Planning Commission on November 21, 2024.

Alexander Hamilton
Interim Planning Commission Secretary

Planning Commission, November 25, 2024  Page 2 of 2
   MINUTES OF THE SPECIAL MEETING
  NORWALK PLANNING COMMISSION
  NORWALK, CALIFORNIA
  OCTOBER 23, 2024

The meeting was called to order by Vice Chair Apodaca at 6:00 p.m., in the Norwalk City
Hall, Council Chambers, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Present were
Commissioner Barragan, Commissioner Nuno, Commissioner Vernola-Salas, and Vice
Chair Apodaca. Chair Lopez was absent. Also present were Alex Hamilton, Interim
Director of Community Development; Gloria V. Ramirez, Deputy City Attorney; Nancy
Lee, Development Services Manager; Gabriel Salazar, Senior Planner; Sophia Tatlyan,
Contract Senior Planner; and Ruth Hoffmann, Administrative Secretary.

MEETING MINUTES

The Planning Commission approved the minutes of the Special Planning Commission
Meetings of June 26 and July 10, 2024, with Commissioners Nuno and Vernola-Salas
abstaining as they were not on the Commission at that time.

ZONING TEXT AMENDMENT NO. 2024-05
To amend various sections of Title 17 the Norwalk Municipal Code to update the
City’s Density Bonus ordinance and update the definition of “Family”.

Vice Chair Apodaca opened the public hearing.

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Senior Planner Salazar
presented a report stating that this zoning text amendment is a request to amend various
sections of Title 17 of the Norwalk Municipal Code to update the city's Density Bonus
ordinance and the definition of “Family” to ensure compliance with the State Density
Bonus law which was established in 2014; that this law established consistent objectives,
policies, regulations, development and design standards, as well as review criteria for
implementing density bonus requirements for eligible projects; that the Density Bonus
ordinance is a mechanism to allow developers to obtain favorable local developer
requirements in exchange for builder building affordable units; that the Density Bonus
allows for greater density than permitted in the underlying zone, and that concessions or
incentives are offered in order to achieve the affordable units.

Further, he presented slides showing the allowable maximum density dwelling units per
acre as follows: In the R-2 zone on a 9,000 square foot minimum lot, 16 dwelling units,
and 22 dwelling units in the R-3 zone; that on a 25,000 square foot minimum lot in the
R-4, C-1, C-3, C&O and P/O zones between 23 and 30 density dwelling units; that in
Specific Plan Area (SPA) Nos. 2 and 3, up to 16 dwelling units, and for SPA Nos. 1, 4, 5,
6, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 14 the maximum density allowed will be determined by plans and
designs that meet all open space, parking, setback and dwelling unit area requirements,
with consideration given to the height of the building(s), whether parking is attached to
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 2
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

each unit, grouped or provided underground, and other design features of the proposed
development.

Senior Planner Salazar shared that a project that has exercised and benefited from the
current Density Bonus ordinance is Mercy Housing’s Veterans Villas (60 dwelling units)
located at 13601 San Antonio Drive; that this project was approved by the Planning
Commission on January 8, 2020 and by the City Council on January 21, 2020; that,
without the density bonus, 45 units were permitted; that the concessions granted to this
project was a reduction in the minimum required open space, a reduction in the minimum
required landscaping, an increase in the maximum allowed building height, and trash
storage areas.

Continuing with his presentation, Senior Planner Salazar stated that another project that
has benefited from this ordinance is “The Views”, 14807 Pioneer Boulevard, a 62-unit
development of which 6 units are designated for very low-income households (46 units
without the Density Bonus); that the concessions granted were a reduction in the
minimum required open space and landscaping; an increase in the maximum allowed
building height; a reduction in the minimum allowed side building setback; and an
application of the Alternative Parking Standards pursuant to NMC Section 17.04.235.I.2.

Senior Planner Salazar indicated that the City’s 6th Cycle Housing Element Update
adopted in February of 2023 requires the City to update the existing Density Bonus
ordinance for compliance with State law; that, in addition, the city is also required to
amend the current definition of “Family”; that the proposed text amendment accomplishes
the following: Updates eligibility, procedural, and development standard requirements;
removes existing process requirements; adds new incentives, waivers, and reductions;
modifies the list of definitions for density bonus, and modifies the city’s Review Authority
Table (NMC 17.02.105); that, in addition, it ensures that the ordinance is in compliance
with the State Density Bonus law requirements, and promotes affordable housing
development; incentivizes the development of affordable housing to developers; that the
Density Bonus is an important incentive to enable more affordable housing opportunities;
and that other factors impact the potential for development, such as land cost,
construction cost, labor cost, and market demand.

Further, Mr. Salazar stated that to codify the proposed zoning text amendments, the
following actions are necessary: That the current Density Bonus (NMC 17.04.235)
ordinance be repealed; that a new Article V “Supplemental Regulations” NMC section be
created and included in Chapter 17; that NMC Section 17.04.400 in Chapter 17.04 titled
“Density Bonus” be created; that the definition of “Family” be updated to be more
inclusive, non-discriminatory and eliminates the exclusion of nuisance; that, as he stated,
the proposed text amendment accomplishes the following: that it updates the eligibility
procedure and development standard requirements; that it removes existing process
requirements; that it adds new incentives, waivers and reductions and modifies the list of
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 3
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

definitions for Density Bonus as well as modifying the city’s Review Authority Table; and
that staff recommends that the Planning Commission adopt Resolution No. 24-11 to
recommend approval to City Council for Zoning Text Amendment No. 2024-05; and
consider and find that the project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) Common Sense Exemption.

Commission Nuno asked how does the new definition of “Family” compare to the previous
definition, how does it make it more inclusive, and and how does it compare to the
definition used by surrounding cities.

Interim Director Hamilton stated that while they are researching the previous definition of
“Family”, the proposed definition complies with the State law; and that every city is
required to be in compliance with the State Density Bonus law.

Vice Chair Apodaca indicated that on Page 6 of the Legislative Draft the definition of
“Family” means one or more persons living together as a single housekeeping unit in a
single dwelling unit, and that the following phrase has been added: “with common access
to and common use of all living, kitchen and eating areas within the dwelling unit.”

Commissioner Nuno stated that her second question concerns the incentives for the
zoning text amendment. She asked how would these incentives affect the current status
of the city’s Housing Element, and would the city have control over where they allow
housing projects.

Interim Director Hamilton indicated that the intent of the ordinance is to apply to the
current residential zones within the city and to the residential uses that are permitted in
the various Specific Plans, as well as in the areas where mixed-use would be allowed, to
make it consistent with State law; and that this is another State mandate. Further, he
shared that every affordable housing project he worked with in other cities had multiple
layers of funding and that they have to layer up the funding; that it is not uncommon for
an affordable housing project to have four or five different funding sources; that it typically
takes four to five years to get the funding lined up to get a project built; that as it relates
to the Mercy Housing project, even with the incentives, the City had to help with the land;
and that he believes that the incentives are not anything to be too concerned about
because there are other forces at work to make these housing projects come to fruition.

Commissioner Barragan complimented staff on putting together this detailed report.

As there were no persons wishing to present testimony, Vice Chair Apodaca closed the
public hearing.

Commissioners Barragan, Nuno and Vernola-Salas indicated that they had no further
questions or comments.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 4
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

Vice Chair Apodaca stated that she, too, appreciated all of the details that were very well
explained; that even though it was a long process, the Mercy Housing development
turned out to be a beautiful project; that she was fortunate enough to visit Mercy Housing’s
other project in El Monte; that she was impressed by it and came away with the belief that
such a project is well worth it, and important to the community. She added that most of
the concessions made do not impact the surrounding areas as much as the parking
concessions which can be extremely impactful and are probably the biggest concern of
the community when these projects come up.

It was moved by Commissioner Barragan and seconded by Vice Chair Apodaca to: (1)
Adopt Resolution No. 24-11 to recommend approval to City Council for Zoning Text
Amendment No. 2024-05; and (2) Consider and find that the project is exempt from the
California Environmental Quality Act pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3)
(Common Sense Exemption), where it can be seen with certainty there is no possibility
that the activity in question may have significant effect on the environment.

ON ROLL CALL VOTE
AYES:  Commissioner Barragan, Commissioner Nuno, Commissioner Vernola-
  Salas and Vice Chair Apodaca
NOES:  None
ABSENT: Chair Lopez

ACCESSORY DWELLING UNIT ORDINANCE UPDATE SESSION WORKSHOP

Interim Director Hamilton stated that the city adopted its first Accessory Dwelling Unit
(ADU) ordinance in 2018; that, since then, there have been many amendments by the
State; that staff is trying to keep the Commission up to date on all the actions that the
State has taken and what staff is seeing in Norwalk on a daily basis, as well as the
limitations they are operating under as it relates to ADUs; that where there are areas of
concern, and the City has objective standards that are applied citywide, they might be
able to be a little more restrictive, but only if the city could point to something that is in
place citywide, not just as it relates to ADUs. Interim Director Hamilton provided examples
stating that, for instance, if ADUs are allowed in the front yard setback and they have a
citywide standard for line-of-sight provision if backing out of the driveway, they might be
able to adopt this in some form or fashion.

Contract Senior Planner Tatlyan shared that they have numerous slides for this
presentation. She stated that ADUs are independent accessory living facilities that meet
the following criteria: They may be converted from an existing living space, garage, or an
accessory structure attached or detached from a primary dwelling; that they contain an
independent kitchen, bathroom, and exterior entrance; that they are typically between
150 square feet and 1,200 square feet in size; and that they tend to have separate utilities
and addresses. She presented slides showing examples of various ADUs that may be
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 5
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

created within existing living spaces, including basements or attics; that other examples
shown are garage conversions, ADUs built in the rear of a property, and an attached ADU
where the ADU shares a common wall with a single-family home.

Continuing with her presentation, Contract Senior Planner Tatlyan indicated that in 2018,
the City updated its Municipal Code to comply with the State law at the time; that in 2019,
the State adopted a slew of new ADU laws that pretty much eroded most local control
over certain types of ADU developments; that most notably was AB 68, which required
cities to allow detached ADUs, ADU conversions, Junior ADUs and ADUs with multiple
family structures; that, in summary these laws made it easier for ADU construction by
removing owner-occupancy requirements, eliminating or capping fees, and streamlining
the ADU approval process; that these laws also allowed for separate sale of ADUs under
certain conditions, and invalidated restrictive covenants in common interest
developments; that between 2020 and 2022, the State further facilitated development and
rental of ADUs by prohibiting unreasonable restrictions in common interest developments
and review, and mandating timely approval of ADU applications; that, additionally, these
laws allow for the separate sale of ADUs, streamline the permitting processes, support
the subdivision of single-family lots and two-unit developments; that over the last two
years, new laws were also approved to continue the support, development, and flexibility
with ADU construction; that these laws mandated pre-approval programs for cities,
permanently prohibited owner-occupancy requirements, allowed for the separate sale of
ADUs as condominiums and streamlined the permitting process by increasing height
limits and consolidating existing laws; that, additionally, they extended amnesty for
unpermitted ADUs and expanded ministerial approval for detached ADUs on multiple
family structures.

Further, Ms. Tatlyan stated that these ADU laws removed local control in a lot of ways as
to how the city regulates ADUs as ADUs now must be permitted in all zones were
residential uses are allowed; and that in 2019 they had mandates, certain types of ideas,
that the city needed to approve, which she is referring to in her presentation as “exempt”
ADUs; that exempt ADUs must be permitted; that they have no control over parking
replacement requirements; that setbacks are required as prescribed by the State; that
review times must be approved or denied within 60 days; and that they cannot delay the
approval of ADUs due to Code Enforcement violations or nonconforming issues.

Continuing with her presentation, Ms. Tatlyan shared that there is a new law for Junior
Accessory Dwelling Units (JADUs); that this is a specific type of conversion of existing
space (not more than 500 square feet) contained entirely within an existing or proposed
single-family residence; that they may include separate sanitation facilities, or may share
sanitation facilities with the existing structure; that they have a kitchen and exterior
entrance independent of the single family dwelling; that there is an owner-occupancy
requirement; and that JADUs are considered exempt by the State.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 6
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

Ms. Tatlyan next commented on numerous slides showing examples of before and after
renderings of detached/attached ADUs, Multi-Family Residential (MFR) ADUs, etc.
Further, she stated that, for example, if there is a converted garage with a 150 square
foot addition, State law allows a maximum allowable expansion of 150 feet for ingress
and egress with a conversion to an ADU; that regarding height, the maximum for a
detached ADU is 18 feet if the detached ADU with a single-family or multi-family structure
is within one-half mile walking distance of a major transit stop or a high quality transit
corridor; that an additional 2 feet in height is allowed to accommodate a roof pitch on the
ADU that is aligned with the roof pitch of the primary dwelling unit; that an 18 foot high
maximum is allowed for a detached ADU with a multi-story, multi-family residence; and
25 feet or the height limitation in the underlying zone for an attached ADU, whichever is
less.

The next item discussed was the meaning of a “Major Transit Stop”. Ms. Tatlyan shared
that this is a site containing any of the following: Rail or bus rapid transit station; ferry
terminal served by either a bus or rail transit service; or the intersection of two or more
major bus routes with a frequency of service interval of 15 minutes or less during the
morning and afternoon peak commute periods; that a “High-quality transit corridor” means
a corridor with fixed route bus service with service intervals no longer than 15 minutes
during peak commute hours. The next slide showed a High Quality Transit Area Map
containing the locations of major transit stops or high quality transit corridors; that the
areas shown in blue are buffers that may allow detached ADUs between 18 feet to 20
feet, and 4-feet from the side and rear property lines; that the reason the height is
important is because the 18 foot to 20 foot height range could allow up to two-story ADUs.

Ms. Tatlyan commented on the parking requirements stating that one parking stall is
required typically for an ADU, unless it is exempt per State law; that there are quite a few
exemptions, the first exemption concerns ADUs that are within one-half mile walking
distance of public transit; that it is important to note that the public transit is different from
a major transit stop; that the other exemptions pertain to ADUs located in a significant
historic district and if an ADU is part of a proposed or existing primary residence or an
accessory structure, when on-street parking permits are required but not offered to the
occupant of the ADU or when there is a car-share vehicle located within one block of the
ADU; that it should be noted that in the previous Municipal Code no parking was required
for ADUs; that the most significant is the one-half mile walking distance from public transit
as the definition just means any bus shelter or bus stop; and that as shown on the map,
a majority of the city has the benefit of a parking exemption.

The next item covered were the non-exempt ADUs. Ms. Tatlyan indicated that these are
ADUs up to 1,000 square feet for studio or one-bedroom floor plans; up to 1,200 square
feet for two-bedroom floor plans; that they must meet the applicable height allowance and
on-site parking requirements with required 4-foot setbacks on the side and the rear; and
that the city can impose additional objective standards to these types of ADUs.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 7
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

Ms. Tatlyan commented on the number of ADU applications received by the Planning
Department between 2018 and 2024; that in 2018 and 2019 there were about 3
applications submitted for each of those years; that in 2020 the number was below 10;
that in 2021 that number increased to 29; that in 2023, 209 applications were received,
while in 2024 the number received to date is 158. Further, she stated that the Planning
staff receives daily calls on this topic; that this month out of 369 inquiries about 111 of
those pertained to ADU development standards and the process of applying for one,
which comes out to about 30% of all received communications; and that in 2023/24, the
Building Department reported that 108 ADUs were finaled.

The next topic pertained to the adverse impacts of ADUs which have had an impact on
parking. Ms. Tatlyan shared that as she mentioned before, State law does not really
require much parking for ADUs and, in combination, does not require to replace any lost
parking; that there are ADU plans that show no parking on site or complete reduction of
parking. Further, she stated that they have received an increased request to build two-
story ADUs; that these detached ADUs just had to meet a 4-foot rear setback and height
limitation; that staff is concerned with the construction of these two-story ADUs as it does
impact surrounding neighbors and their privacy; that staff has also received requests to
build ADUs in the R-H (Residential Horse) property zone; and that this could reduce or
eliminate the possibility of future animal permits based on the plans presented.

Ms. Tatlyan commented on reduced open space. She stated that State law requires them
to approve at least one 800 square foot detached ADU, regardless of lot size; that this
has an impact on the backyard space or the open rear yard areas for single-family
residential homes and line-of-sight; that regarding poor architectural design and
compatibility with primary dwelling, subjective design standards are not allowed in the
ADU review per State law; that regarding loop holes, they have discovered that there is
a limitation on additions, which she explained; that another concern are requests to
legalize garage conversions that were built before 2018; that this is a State mandate; and
that they do have a process in order to approve those.

Further, she stated that her presentation is the city’s interpretation of the areas of flexibility
that they have; that the Department of Housing and Community Development will review
any future ADU ordinance after its adoption within 60 days for compliance with State law.

Ms. Tatlyan shared that the following are things to consider when they craft the ADU
ordinance: Increased height allowances; eliminate parking requirements altogether;
single-story limitation, just allowing one-story ADUs; ADU conversions with an addition
that exceeds 150 square feet; covenants limiting future expansion; minimum distance
between structures; front door orientation; screening of exterior stairwells; landscaping;
setback incentives for two-story structures; opaque, frosted glass windows on second
levels, including window placements and window size; lighting; specific materials and
finishes that will help with matching the front home with the rear ADU and vice versa;
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 8
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

building articulation; citywide development standards for all residential zones; reducing
the allowable encroachment; patio covers; lot coverage and floor area ratio requirements
in residential zones citywide; line-of-sight in commercial and residential zones; and open
space requirements.

Continuing with her presentation, Ms. Tatlyan stated that the Planning Department is the
first step for any ADU inquiries; that the proposed plans are submitted to the Building
Division who makes sure that the plans get the proper review and approval of other
outside agencies and departments; that, in addition, the Engineering Department reviews
the plans, verifies if there are any grading permits required or drainage plans that need
to be included; that they verify that the Los Angeles County Fire Department has reviewed
the plans for consistency with their requirements, including the Sanitation District, School
District fees, and making sure the local utilities are aware of the ADU project and are in
line with their regulations as well; that they have seen ADUs being built too close to power
lines; that part of the review process is making sure that the utility company is aware of
this so they can make sure that these uses are a safe enough distance away from utility
lines.

Commissioner Barragan stated that her concern is with parking.

Vice Chair Apodaca also voiced her concern with parking for multiple dwellings as a
number of ADUs can be added. She stated that the lack of parking is already impacting
all of the city’s neighborhoods, especially on those streets where parking permits are
required.

Interim Director Hamilton stated that the State law, in essence, is stripping away the
parking requirements from all cities; that the city is working on a city-wide parking study
which still needs to be vetted; and that, at best, the city needs to have an objective
standard that they can apply city-wide.

Ms. Tatlyan shared that they have not received too many multiple-family applications; and
that the majority are from single-family neighborhoods.

Commissioner Vernola-Salas commented on condominiums, and she asked if it is correct
that they can convert their garage into an ADU. Ms. Tatlyan stated that it is her
understanding that CC&Rs do not supersede State law.

Commissioner Vernola-Salas asked if an ADU can sit closer to the State required 4-foot
property line, Ms. Tatlyan stated that it has to be at least 4-feet from the side and the rear
property line; that it can be up to zero feet for converted ADUs; and that the city does not
have control over ADU conversions if they are less than 4-feet from the property line.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 9
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

Commissioner Vernola-Salas commented on the height of an ADU, and she asked if it is
correct that new construction of an ADU in the back yard can now be two-stories in height
per State law, even if the front house is a single-story dwelling, Ms. Tatlyan shared that
the State law has a height limit; and that without a zoning ordinance staff can defer to,
the city can only deny it based on the height.

Vice Chair Apodaca commented on the requirement for ADUs that are within one-half of
a mile walking distance of a major transit stop or a high-quality transit corridor, and she
asked if it is correct that the structure in the back can be larger than the main house. Ms.
Tatlyan replied that a detached ADU is not based on the size of the main dwelling.

Ms. Tatlyan indicated that the height allowance from 16-feet to 18-feet has opened
opportunities for two-story ADUs; that detached ADUs are different than attached ADUs;
that an attached ADU technically cannot exceed 800 square feet, or 50 percent of the
size of the main house, but it also can fall below the minimum size requirement for an
ADU of 800 square feet; that an attached ADU can be 800 square feet and the front house
could be 600 square feet; that for a new detached ADU, the limit is 1,200 square feet
combined; and that they could set a maximum size of 1,000 square feet based on
bedroom count; that for a one-bedroom studio, for example, they can cap it at 1,000
square feet and not be in violation; and that for a two-bedroom house, it can go up to
1,200 square feet.

Interim Director Hamilton shared that they are talking about exempt versus non-exempt;
that exempt means that it has to be approved per State standards; that non-exempt gives
them potentially a little bit more discretion; that regarding the maximum 4-foot setback for
new construction, this also kind of works as a minimum when existing garages get
converted as sometimes the garage slab needs to be addressed to comply with the code
by providing a vapor barrier or fire-resistant construction if they are too close to the
property line; that they are trying to be as strict as they can for items safety-related; and
that as stated by staff, they are engaging in interdepartmental review and coordination of
ADU applications, as previously utilities might not necessarily be aware of any issues until
the permits are issued.

Commissioner Nuno asked what is the biggest challenge for staff since the State
standards have been passed. Ms. Tatlyan replied that the lack of an ordinance has been
a big obstacle as it is up to staff now to interpret State law as it is being introduced; that
residents come in and say their neighbor was allowed to do a certain thing, but now they
are not allowed to do the same; and that it is critical for staff and the community that an
ordinance be adopted.

Interim Director Hamilton provided examples of what an applicant in the multi-family zone
tried to do with ADUs, and he stated that people are trying to push the envelope; and that
the ordinance needs to be updated with subjective standards to protect the community.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 10
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

Vice Chair Apodaca brought up the question of having separate addresses for the ADUs,
and she asked if, eventually, this could become a whole separate piece of property, and
if they are going to have the ability to sell ADUs separately.

Interim Director Hamilton indicated that this refers to SB 9, or lot split, which has been in
effect for about three years; and that this is a separate discussion that staff would like to
have with the Commission.

Commissioner Nuno stated that she is glad that staff brought up the issue about sewer
and water lines; and she asked if the City’s infrastructure can sustain these ADUs.

Interim Director Hamilton indicated that the City is working on a citywide master sewer
plan to address those issues.

In response to Commissioner Nuno’s inquiry if staff knows whether the majority of the
ADU applications received were from residents or from investors who do not reside in the
city, Ms. Tatlyan replied that every building application requires the property owner’s
signature; and that they would need to look up this information. Further, she stated that
with Junior ADUs, there is a requirement that the property owner live on the property if
they want to rent out the facility; and that, originally, this was also a requirement of ADUs,
but that the State removed it.

In reply to Vice Chair Apodaca’s comment if, as mentioned by staff, an ADU is being
located too close to a power line, Interim Director Hamilton stated that, hopefully, it will
get caught through the review period; that now, when residents come in with a concept
plan and talk with a planner about what they can and cannot do, they are trying to flag
those issues early to prevent such things from happening.

Ms. Tatlyan asked the Commission if they have any thoughts or suggestions on any of
the slides shown that they can incorporate into the city standards, for example, the two-
story ADU versus the one-story ADU.

Vice Chair Apodaca stated that she would be for a one-story ADU if it does not violate the
State law; that she was on the committee when they originally came up with conditions
for regulating ADUs; that their intent was to try to have these ADUs blend into the
neighborhoods instead of being monstrosities, and that those units should have the least
impact on this community. She added that she likes the line-of-sight option, and not
allowing ADUs in front yards, but that they cannot control parking.

Commissioner Vernola-Salas indicated that the ADUs not have a single address; that
they could just add a “-1” or “B” to differentiate from the main address so the lot would not
be split.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 11
Minutes of the Special Meeting  October 23, 2024

Vice Chair Apodaca stated that she has seen cities adding a “1/2” number to the address;
and that this might be best for tax purposes.

Interim Director Hamilton stated that, again, they can come back to the Commission for

RECOMMENDATION

That the Planning Commission:

1. Adopt Resolution No. 24-12 finding that the City of Norwalk’s acquisition of 13200
Bloomfield Avenue (APN No. 8045-008-902) in the City of Norwalk to be in conformity with
the General Plan; and
2. Consider and find that the project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
pursuant to AB 518.

REQUEST

California Government Code Section 65402 requires that the acquisition of real property
be submitted to and reported upon by the Planning Agency (Planning Commission) as to
conformity with the adopted General Plan. The City is requesting a finding of General Plan
conformity (Finding of Conformity) for the proposed acquisition of 13200 Bloomfield Avenue
(APN No. 8045-008-902) (Subject Site). The Planning Commission's review for General Plan
conformity will be forwarded to the City Council for its consideration of the property acquisition
at a future date.

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND

On October 2, 2018, the City adopted an Economic Development Opportunities Plan that
identified various areas throughout the City that could promote economic development. The
site is a key node identified for its redevelopment potential given its location, size, and access
to transportation. The plan was updated October 17, 2023.

The Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan is a City staff-initiated project, involves a 32.3-acre
site generally situated between Imperial Highway to the north, the Union Pacific Railroad to the
east, and Bloomfield Avenue to the west.

The project site was originally developed in 1943 as an all-male youth correctional facility
operated by the California Youth Authority (CYA). In 2011, the CYA facility operations ceased,
and the project site remained vacant until 2019, at which time the facility was temporarily
utilized by the California Department of State Hospitals (DSH) due to the Coronavirus Disease
(COVID-19) pandemic. The project site was being used by the DSH as a temporary satellite
mental hospital facility to mitigate the effects of “surge space” at local state hospitals until early
2022. The facility was housing primarily COVID-negative mental forensic inmates; however,
all inmates have been moved out of the facility. Currently, the Department of General Services
(DGS), who currently owns the property, to use the facility on an as-needed basis.

Government Code Section 11011.28(e) (AB 518), which was enacted in 2020 and effective
January 1, 2021, authorizes the DGS, until January 1, 2025, to sell the property to the City of
Norwalk at fair market value upon terms and conditions the Director determines are in the best
interests of the State. The bill authorizes DGS, notwithstanding those provisions, to sell the
property below fair market value for purposes of providing housing to persons and families of
low or moderate income. The bill, after January 1, 2025, authorizes the Director to dispose of
the property in accordance with specified procedures and priorities otherwise applicable to the
disposal of surplus property by DGS.

Under the provisions of AB 518, which amended Government Code Section 11011.28, the City
is pursuing the purchase of the project site from the State as a part of the implementation of
the Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan allows a mixed-use development with up to 66,647
square feet of neighborhood commercial uses, 13,500 square feet of active commercial uses,
a hotel with up to 150 rooms, up to 770 housing units, and 3.7 acres of open space/parkland
uses.

Conformity with the General Plan

On July 10, 2024, the Planning Commission recommended that the City Council approve the
Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan.

On November 19, 2024, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 24-58 (Final Environmental
Impact Report State Clearinghouse No. 2022070103), Resolution No. 24-56 (General Plan
Amendment No. 2022-01 (2024-01)), Resolution No. 24-57 (Zone Change No. 2022-01 (2024-
02)), Ordinance No. 24-1754 (Zoning Text Amendment No. 2022-02 (2024-04)) to establish
Specific Plan Area No. 17, the Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan.

ANALYSIS

The Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA) is mandated by State Housing Law as part
of the periodic process of updating local housing elements of the General Plan. RHNA
quantifies the need for housing within each jurisdiction during specified planning periods. In
March 2021, Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) adopted its 6th cycle
RHNA allocation plan, which covers the planning period October 2021 through October 2029.

For the 6th cycle, SCAG received a need of 1,341,827 housing units, which was distributed to
all 197 SCAG jurisdictions. City’s RNHA obligation is 5,034 units.

The finding of conformity for the acquisition of the Subject Site is made pursuant to the
requirements of the Government Code Section 65402 and is based upon the following:

Conformity with the Housing Element

DGS has required that development of the site comply with Government Code Section 37364,
which requires that a minimum of 40 percent of the units built on the Subject Site to be
designated as affordable. As such, acquisition of the Subject Site by the City would further
goals and policies of the City’s Housing Element by increasing affordable housing
opportunities, increase homeownership, create safe and integrated neighborhoods, encourage
and facilitate a range of housing to encourage a variety of housing types to meet the existing
and future needs of City residents, and assist in the development of adequate housing and
provide resources to meet the needs of low-and moderate income households.

Additionally, the Subject Site is listed under the Housing Elements Sites Inventory. The
development of up to 770 new residential housing units would assist the City in meeting its
RHNA obligation while eliminating blight and enhancing public safety.
 Finding the City of Norwalk Acquisition  Page 4
Of 13200 Bloomfield Avenue to be in  November 25, 2024
Conformity with the General Plan

Conformity with the General Plan

The proposed acquisition of the Subject Site is in conformity with the Land Use Element
Objectives and policies in that the acquisition would provide for a larger comprehensive
development along the City’s major arterials which will enhance the overall character of the
streetscape and will include adequate parking, buffering and landscaping (Objective and Policy
4a).

ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT

The Finding of Conformity is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”)
pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3) (Common Sense Exemption), which states
that an activity is covered by the common sense exemption that CEQA only applies to projects
that have the potential for causing a significant effect on the environment. Where it can be
seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the activity in question may have a significant
effect on the environment, the activity is not subject to CEQA review.

The finding of conformity is limited to legal findings and will not result in a physical change in
the environment and none of the exceptions under CEQA Guidelines Section 15300.2 apply.

Moreover, Government Code Section 11011.28(e) (AB 518) exempts the acquisition of the
Subject Site from CEQA.

Lastly, the Finding of Conformity is consistent with those actions taken by the City Council on
November 19, 2024 where the City Council certified the Final EIR and approved a Mitigation
and Monitoring and Reporting Program, and adopted a Statement of Overriding Considerations
in connection with the Norwalk Transit Specific Plan through City Council Resolution No. 24-
58. The acquisition of the Subject Site by the City was evaluated and contemplated by the
Final EIR and is in compliance with the requirements of CEQA.

SUMMARY

The City Council will take action on a Purchase and Sales Agreement with the DGS to acquire
the Subject Site at a future date. The Planning Commission is required to render its report as
to conformity with the General Plan prior to City Council’s consideration of a Purchase and
Sales agreement to acquire the Subject Site. Staff recommends that the Planning Commission
find the City’s proposed acquisition of the Subject Site is in conformity with the City’s General
Plan. This staff report and Planning Commission Resolution No. 24-12 will serve as that report
if approved by the Planning Commission.
